name: Ida B. Wells
aliases: Ida B. Wells-Barnett; Ida Bell Wells-Barnett; Ida Bell Wells; Iola
description: Ida B. Wells (born Ida Bell Wells, July 16, 1862, in Holly Springs, Mississippi; died 1931) was an investigative journalist, newspaper owner and editor, anti-lynching investigator, and organizer whose career CTL documents across five research programs. By 1889 she was editor and part-owner of the Memphis Free Speech and Headlight, writing as "Iola." After the March 9, 1892 lynching of Thomas Moss, Calvin McDowell, and William Stewart, her newspaper office was destroyed in May 1892 and she was exiled from Memphis; her pamphlets Southern Horrors (1892) and The Red Record (1895) pioneered data-driven anti-lynching investigation. In Chicago she owned and edited the Chicago Conservator (1895–1897), married Ferdinand L. Barnett in 1895, founded the Negro Fellowship League in 1910, and co-founded the Alpha Suffrage Club. Her Chicago residence, the Ida B. Wells-Barnett House at 3624 S. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Dr., is a designated Chicago Landmark, and CTL's dedicated dossier (CTL-RD-PER-000001) grades her claims individually.

name: I Feel for You
description: I Feel for You is Chaka Khan's 1984 solo album on Warner Bros. Records, released after the dissolution of Rufus, the band she had fronted alongside her solo career from 1978 to 1983. Its title track is Khan's version of a song Prince wrote and first recorded on his 1979 album Prince; Khan's recording adds a rap introduction by Melle Mel of Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five and a harmonica part by Stevie Wonder, and it became an international hit that relaunched her mainstream career. The song reached No. 3 on the Billboard Hot 100, topped the U.S. R&B and dance charts and the U.K. singles chart, and earned Grammy Awards for both Prince, as songwriter, and Khan, as vocalist. The album also carries the ballad 'Through the Fire' and the singles 'This Is My Night' and 'Eye to Eye,' and it stands as the mainstream breakthrough of Khan's solo career.

name: Ida B. Wells-Barnett House
aliases: Ida B. Wells House; Wells-Barnett House
description: The Ida B. Wells-Barnett House, at 3624 S. Martin Luther King Jr. Drive in the Douglas community area of Chicago's South Side, is a three-story ashlar granite residence in the Romanesque Revival style popular around 1890. The National Park Service nomination records that it was built about 1889–90, to a design attributed to architect Joseph Thain, and that Ida B. Wells and her husband, attorney Ferdinand Lee Barnett, moved there in October 1919, raising their four children in the house. The nomination states the couple sold the building in March 1929 and moved to smaller quarters; other summaries give the residence as 1919 to 1930, a variance this record shows rather than blends. Wells, born into slavery in Mississippi in 1862, continued her writing and anti-lynching activism from Chicago and was a founding organizer of the NAACP. The house, subdivided into apartments in later years, is the best preserved of the Chicago addresses associated with her. It was designated a National Historic Landmark and listed on the National Register of Historic Places on May 30, 1974, and designated a Chicago Landmark on October 2, 1995 — two distinct designations in two distinct years.

name: Isiah Thomas
description: Isiah Thomas (born April 30, 1961, in Chicago) is the West Side Chicago point guard who became one of the greatest small guards in basketball history. Raised in poverty on Chicago's West Side and starred at St. Joseph High School in suburban Westchester, he led Indiana University to the 1981 NCAA championship as a sophomore, earning Final Four Most Outstanding Player honors, and was drafted second overall by the Detroit Pistons. He played all thirteen of his NBA seasons in Detroit, leading the 'Bad Boys' Pistons to consecutive championships in 1989 and 1990 and winning Finals MVP in 1990. A twelve-time All-Star who led the league in assists in 1985, he retired with 18,822 points and 9,061 assists as Detroit's franchise leader in both. He was inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in 2000, and Detroit has retired his No. 11.

name: Ice Cube
description: Ice Cube (born O'Shea Jackson on June 15, 1969, in Los Angeles, California) is the rapper, songwriter, actor and producer who wrote much of N.W.A's landmark work and then built one of hip-hop's most durable solo and film careers. After the group C.I.A. (1986), he co-founded N.W.A in 1987 with Eazy-E and Dr. Dre and wrote most of the lyrics on Straight Outta Compton (1988), the album that carried gangsta rap to a national audience. Following a dispute over the group's management and his earnings, he left N.W.A — reference works differ on whether the departure falls in late 1989 or 1990; the record prints the variance — and released the solo albums AmeriKKKa's Most Wanted (1990), Death Certificate (1991) and The Predator (1992). On screen he debuted as Doughboy in Boyz n the Hood (1991) and co-wrote and starred in Friday (1995), which grew into a franchise. He was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame as a member of N.W.A in 2016.

name: Insecure
description: Insecure, created by Issa Rae and Larry Wilmore and grown from Rae's web series Awkward Black Girl, premiered on HBO in the fall of 2016 — online on September 23 and on the network on October 9 — and ended its run on December 26, 2021, after five seasons following Issa Dee and her friends through the work, rent, and relationships of Black Los Angeles in their late twenties and thirties. It is a Peabody Award-winning series; the American Film Institute named it one of the top ten television programs of 2017; and its fourth season drew eight Primetime Emmy nominations, including the series' first nomination for Outstanding Comedy Series, with Rae herself earning three Emmy and three Golden Globe lead-actress nominations across the run. Its lineage is the shelf's own: Rae has cited Living Single openly, and Insecure carried the friendship-sitcom form into the premium-cable era — shorter seasons, single camera, a city shot like a hometown rather than a backdrop. The graph files it as the 2010s' second anchor beside Black-ish: the broadcast form's intimate, independent sibling.

name: Issa Rae
description: Issa Rae (born Jo-Issa Rae Diop, January 12, 1985, in Los Angeles) is an actress, writer and producer who carried a self-made web series into the center of American television. A Stanford University graduate in African and African-American studies, she created The Misadventures of Awkward Black Girl (2011–2013) and turned it into a New York Times best-selling memoir in 2015. She co-created and starred in HBO's Insecure (2016–2021), a Peabody Award-winning series that brought her multiple Primetime Emmy and Golden Globe nominations. In 2020 she founded HOORAE, a media company spanning film and television production, the Raedio audio label and the ColorCreative management venture. Her film work includes The Hate U Give, The Photograph, Barbie and American Fiction, and the voice of Spider-Woman in Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse. She served as an ambassador for the American Black Film Festival in 2022 and was the first guest on IMO with Michelle Obama. CultureTechLens profiled Rae in Short #100, published October 13, 2026.

name: Isabel Wilkerson
description: Isabel Wilkerson (born 1961 in Washington, D.C.) is an American journalist and author, and a daughter of the Great Migration her parents made from the South. A Howard University graduate who edited the student newspaper The Hilltop, she became Chicago bureau chief of The New York Times. In 1994 she won the Pulitzer Prize for Feature Writing for coverage of the 1993 Midwestern floods and a profile of a ten-year-old caring for his siblings, becoming the first African American woman to win a Pulitzer Prize in journalism. She spent fifteen years interviewing more than 1,200 people for The Warmth of Other Suns (2010), her history of the Great Migration, which won the National Book Critics Circle Award for Nonfiction. President Barack Obama awarded her the National Humanities Medal in 2016. Her second book, Caste: The Origins of Our Discontents (2020), argues American racial hierarchy is a caste system; it reached No. 1 on The New York Times nonfiction bestseller list, was an Oprah's Book Club selection, and inspired Ava DuVernay's film Origin (2023).

name: Imports Etc.
aliases: Imports Etc Records; Importes, Etc.; Importes Etc.
description: Legendary Chicago record store and hub for house DJs. In the early 1980s, when mainstream stores did not carry 12-inch vinyl singles, Importes Etc. — alongside State Street Records, JR's Music Shop, and Gramaphone Records — was one of the primary Chicago suppliers. Chip E. worked at the store in the early 1980s; bins of music that Frankie Knuckles played at the Warehouse nightclub were labeled 'As Heard at the Warehouse' in the store, shortened to 'House' — Chip E.'s account of the genre name's origin. Knuckles was a regular customer, and an employee who knew his taste curated a special bin of selections for him.

name: Inner City Broadcasting Corporation
description: Pioneering Black-owned broadcast company founded 1970 by Percy Sutton, Clarence Jones and 50+ Black shareholders (Hal Jackson, David Dinkins, Betty Shabazz, Carl McCall, Roberta Flack, Billy Taylor; Dorothy Brunson early executive). First acquisition WLIB-AM (1972, first Black-owned NYC station); WBLS-FM (1974) pioneered urban contemporary under Frankie Crocker. At peak: 18 stations plus Queens/Philadelphia cable franchises; bought the Apollo Theater at bankruptcy sale (1981, $225,000; $20M renovation; reopened 1985; nonprofit takeover 1992). Chapter 11 in 2011 ($254M debt); WBLS/WLIB sold to YMF Media. Second-largest Black-audience broadcaster after Radio One.

name: Institutional Closure
description: Closure (or near-closure) of the Black-led institution holding a collection, converting archives into bankruptcy assets, dispersed property, or unfunded orphans. Documented cases: Johnson Publishing Company Chapter 7 (2019-04-09) with the Ebony/Jet archive auctioned for $30M; JPC's Michigan Avenue HQ sold (2017, $10M); Jet print ended (2014-06); Ebony print suspended (2019-05-24); Chicago Defender print ended (2019-07); Inner City Broadcasting Chapter 11 (2011) with WBLS/WLIB sold; King and King Funeral Home building demolished (2024) after records rescue; African American MDIs fell from 48 (2001) to 21 (2019) per FDIC.

name: Indiana Historical Society
description: Indiana Historical Society (IHS): private nonprofit membership organization founded 1830; oldest state historical society west of the Allegheny Mountains; self-described 'Indiana's Storyteller.' Housed in the Eugene and Marilyn Glick Indiana History Center, 450 W Ohio St, Indianapolis (opened July 1999; 165,000 sq ft). Maintains research library and archives on Indiana and Old Northwest history; appoints/trains the state's 92 county historians. Repository for the King and King Funeral Home records rescued before the building's 2024 demolition.

name: Internet Archive
description: Internet Archive: American nonprofit 501(c)(3) digital library founded 1996-05-10 by Brewster Kahle; mission 'universal access to all knowledge.' HQ 300 Funston Ave, San Francisco (former Fourth Church of Christ, Scientist building, since late 2009). Runs the Wayback Machine (public launch 2001-10-24; 808B+ captures by Jan 2023), Open Library book digitization, Archive-It. National Emergency Library (2020-03-24 to 2020-06-16) drew Hachette v. Internet Archive (S.D.N.Y. 2023-03-25; affirmed 2d Cir. 2024-09). October 2024: DDoS attack plus breach of 31M user accounts. Used by journalists and Wikipedia editors to verify vanished web content - a backstop for Black digital memory (CTL PRESERVE-001: 199,000+ BET.com articles explorer, 2026-09-08; WVON airchecks).

name: Irene McCoy Gaines
description: Social worker, clubwoman, and political organizer (1892-1964). Born in Florida, raised in Chicago; studied social work at Fisk University and the University of Chicago. Stenographer at Cook County Juvenile Court; 1917 director of the Girls' Work Division (War Camp Community Service); industrial secretary of the first Black YWCA branch; Chicago Urban League leader; Cook County Welfare Department social worker for 15 years from 1930. Founded the Chicago Council of Negro Organizations (1939; president 1939-1953, ~100 member orgs); led the 1941 Washington lobbying trip preceding Executive Order 8802; appointed to Hoover's National Committee on Negro Housing (1931), leading to the Ida B. Wells Homes. First Black woman to run for the Illinois legislature (1940); 15th president of the National Association of Colored Women's Clubs (1952-1958); testified at the UN (1947). Died of cancer 1964-04-07. CHA's 151-unit Irene McCoy Gaines Apartments (East Garfield Park) bear her name.

description: ICBC purchases the Apollo Theater at a bankruptcy sale for $225,000; a $20 million renovation follows and the theater reopens in 1985.

name: Inner City Broadcasting files for Chapter 11 (2011)
description: Creditors move ICBC's assets into Chapter 11 over a $254 million debt; the WBLS/WLIB sale to YMF Media follows, ending the Black-ownership era.

name: Internet Archive cyberattack and data breach (2024-10-09)
description: Sustained DDoS attack, website defacement, and breach of 31 million user accounts at the Internet Archive, confirmed by founder Brewster Kahle.

name: Internet Archive National Emergency Library launch (2020-03-24)
description: Internet Archive opens the National Emergency Library with unlimited simultaneous e-book borrowing during COVID-19 library closures; it closes June 16, 2020 after publishers sue.

name: Irene McCoy Gaines leads 1941 Washington lobbying trip
description: Gaines leads a 50-person Chicago delegation to Washington, D.C. to protest discrimination in employment, the Federal Housing Authority, and the military; the activism precedes Executive Order 8802.

name: Indiana Landmarks
description: Statewide historic-preservation nonprofit; its Black Heritage Preservation Program (director Eunice Trotter) received the King and King Funeral Home records in September 2024.

name: Ira Acree
aliases: Rev. Ira Acree; Ira J. Acree
description: Co-chair of the Leaders Network, the Black-pastors organization behind the Leaders Network Credit Union in Chicago's Austin neighborhood; lead pastor of Greater St. John Bible Church, Chicago.

name: Intel Corporation
description: Technology company; Kahlief Adams formerly served as Technical Program Manager in its VR, Gaming & Esports Group.

name: IGN
description: Games media company; Kahlief Adams co-hosts its Podcast Unlocked show.

name: Illinois Office of Comptroller
description: The Illinois Office of Comptroller is the Illinois state office headed by Comptroller Susana A. Mendoza. In October 2022 the office collaborated with the Bronzeville Historical Society to rescue burial records from shuttered Black-owned funeral homes before, in the office's words, 'the historical records were lost forever.' The rescued database exceeds 140,000 burial records, with death records dating to the 1880s; a ten-person Bronzeville Historical Society team led by Society founder Sherry Williams processed them. The collection was transferred to the Vivian G. Harsh Research Collection at the Chicago Public Library's Carter G. Woodson Regional Library. The rescue, announced in the office's October 4, 2022 press release, is documented in CultureTechLens's CTL-DR-PRESERVE-001 as a major preservation intervention for Illinois Black history.

name: Ida B. Wells Just Data Lab
aliases: JUST DATA Lab; Just Data Lab
description: Princeton-based lab founded by Ruha Benjamin in 2018 where activists, technologists, and artists reassess how data can be used for justice.

name: Internet Essentials Chicago launch
description: Internet Essentials Chicago launch is recorded in the CultureTechLens graph as an Event, Provisional, under project TECH-001. Its cited source, the research brief 'Black Chicago Goes Online' (CTL-RB-TECH-000002 v1.0, 2026-10-09), states that Comcast launched Internet Essentials in Chicago for the 2011–12 school year, and that Mayor Rahm Emanuel announced it at the Woodson Library in Washington Heights. Families with children on free school lunch could get service for $9.95 a month and a computer for $149.99. The graph era is given only as 'contemporary'; the brief places the launch in its account of Chicago's institutional broadband on-ramps, alongside the Smart Communities program. No enrollment, eligibility-administration, or outcome figures for the Chicago launch are documented in the corpus, and none are asserted here; the prices are the brief's reported launch terms, carried as reported.

name: Isaac Hayes
description: Isaac Lee Hayes Jr. (August 20, 1942 – August 10, 2008) was a Memphis soul singer, songwriter, composer and producer who helped build the Stax Records sound. Born in Covington, Tennessee, he came to Memphis and joined Stax as a session pianist and staff writer, partnering with David Porter on songs including “Soul Man” and “Hold On, I’m Comin’” for Sam & Dave and “B-A-B-Y” for Carla Thomas. His solo breakthrough, Hot Buttered Soul (1969), remade soul as long-form orchestral music; Black Moses and the Shaft soundtrack followed, and his “Theme from Shaft” won the 1972 Academy Award for Best Original Song. Later generations met him as the voice of Chef on South Park (1997–2006). He was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2002 and, with Porter, the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2005.

name: I’m Still in Love with You
aliases: I'm Still in Love with You
description: I’m Still in Love with You is a studio album by Al Green, released in 1972 on Hi Records, months after Let’s Stay Together. Produced by Willie Mitchell and recorded at Royal Studios in Memphis with the Hi Rhythm Section, it deepens the partnership’s formula: Green’s feather-light tenor and falsetto laid over tight drums, horns, and strings, intimacy engineered like architecture. The title track became one of his defining singles. The album also carries “Love and Happiness,” later one of his most celebrated recordings, and “Look What You Done for Me.” Its cover — Green in a white suit, seated in a white wicker chair — is, as Exclaim! wrote, one of the indelible images of the 1970s. Exclaim! also documents the album reaching number four on the Billboard pop chart. I’m Still in Love with You is the second panel of the diptych — with Let’s Stay Together — on which Green’s claim to the soul pantheon principally rests.

name: Ice Spice
description: Ice Spice, born Isis Naija Gaston in the Bronx, New York, on January 1, 2000, is an American rapper whose rise from college student to national chart presence happened with unusual speed. She attended SUNY Purchase, where she met producer RiotUSA, and began releasing music in 2021. Her 2022 single Munch (Feelin' U) spread widely online and established her relaxed delivery over Bronx drill production. The EP Like..? followed in January 2023, and during that year she placed a remarkable run of collaborations in the Billboard Hot 100 top ten, including Boy's a Liar Pt. 2 with PinkPantheress, a remix of Taylor Swift's Karma, and Barbie World with Nicki Minaj and Aqua for the Barbie film. Her debut studio album Y2K! arrived in July 2024. The Recording Academy gave her four nominations at the 2024 Grammy Awards, including Best New Artist, confirming how quickly a viral local sound had become a mainstream pop-rap career.

name: Invention of the Cotton Gin (1793)
aliases: Cotton Gin; Rise of the Cotton Industry
description: In 1793, working at Mulberry Grove plantation near Savannah, Georgia, Eli Whitney built a working model of the cotton gin, a machine that used rotating teeth and brushes to pull the sticky seeds from short-staple cotton fiber. He applied for a patent on October 28, 1793; it was granted on March 14, 1794. The gin let one worker clean roughly fifty times the cotton possible by hand, and it transformed the American South: short-staple cotton, previously unprofitable, became the region's dominant cash crop, and United States cotton production and exports climbed for the rest of the century. The machine's efficiency ran on enslaved labor — demand for enslaved field workers surged with every new acre planted, and the enslaved population of the United States grew from about 700,000 in 1790 to nearly 4 million by 1860. CTL records the gin under the intake timeline's 'Rise of the Cotton Industry' stop, with the audit's correction: 1793 is the year of the machine, and the machine is what made the rise — and slavery's expansion — possible.

name: Integration of Little Rock Central High School (1957)
aliases: Little Rock Nine; Central High School Integrated; Little Rock Crisis
description: In September 1957, three years after Brown v. Board of Education, nine Black teenagers — the Little Rock Nine — attempted to enroll at Central High School in Little Rock, Arkansas, under a federal desegregation plan. Governor Orval Faubus ordered the Arkansas National Guard to surround the school and turn them away; on September 4 the Guard blocked Elizabeth Eckford, who had not received word of the group's changed plans and faced the mob alone. After a federal court ordered the Guard withdrawn and a riot answered the students' first entry on September 23, President Dwight D. Eisenhower federalized the Arkansas National Guard and sent the 101st Airborne Division to Little Rock. On September 25, 1957, soldiers escorted the Nine into Central High, where they endured a school year of harassment under military protection. Faubus closed Little Rock's high schools entirely the following year rather than integrate them. The crisis was the first great test of whether Brown would be enforced, and its answer — federal troops, or nothing — instructed both sides of the decade to come.

name: Integration of the University of Mississippi (1962)
aliases: Ole Miss Integration; Ole Miss Crisis of 1962; Integration of Ole Miss
description: On September 30, 1962, as James Meredith (CTL-E-5385) arrived on the University of Mississippi campus at Oxford under escort, a segregationist mob rioted through the night against the federal marshals protecting him; two people were killed and hundreds injured before Army troops restored order. Meredith, an Air Force veteran, had applied to the all-white university in 1961 and sued for admission after its refusal; Mississippi's governor, Ross Barnett, personally blocked his registration attempts in defiance of federal court orders. President Kennedy federalized the Mississippi National Guard and sent marshals and regular troops to enforce the courts. On October 1, 1962, Meredith registered — the first Black student enrolled at the University of Mississippi — and he persisted through a year of ostracism and harassment to graduate in August 1963. The Ole Miss crisis was the gravest federal-state confrontation over desegregation since Little Rock, and it demonstrated, at the cost of two lives, that enrollment orders would be enforced at bayonet point when states made bayonets necessary.

name: In Living Color
description: In Living Color, created, written, and headlined by Keenen Ivory Wayans and produced by Ivory Way Productions with 20th Television, aired on Fox from April 15, 1990, to May 19, 1994 — five seasons of sketch comedy built, pointedly, as the alternative: where the era's established sketch shows fielded mostly white casts, Wayans built a majority-Black company and let it aim at everything, including Black America's own pieties. It won the Primetime Emmy for Outstanding Variety, Music or Comedy Series in 1990, its first year. Its 1992 live Super Bowl counter-programming special drew ratings large enough to change how the NFL and networks treat halftime itself. Its alumni roll is a generation: Jamie Foxx, Jim Carrey, David Alan Grier, Tommy Davidson, the Wayans family, and the Fly Girl dancers choreographed by Rosie Perez, among them Jennifer Lopez. The production archive is held by the National Comedy Center — an institution's judgment this graph echoes: In Living Color is the sketch shelf's cornerstone, the show that made Fox's Sunday night a Black cultural broadcast.

name: Isaiah Rashad
description: Isaiah Rashad (born Isaiah Rashad Joel McClain, May 16, 1991, in Chattanooga, Tennessee) is an American rapper and singer, and a founding member of the Chattanooga hip-hop collective TheHouse. Raised on his stepbrother's copy of Outkast's ATLiens, he broke out on the 2012 Smoker's Club Tour and signed with Top Dawg Entertainment in March 2013. His debut EP Cilvia Demo (2014) reached No. 40 on the Billboard 200 and landed him in XXL's 2014 Freshman Class. The Sun's Tirade (2016) peaked at No. 17 and was later certified gold; The House Is Burning (2021), his Warner Records debut, followed a five-year hiatus. His third studio album, It's Been Awful — the subject of CTL Short #45 — arrived in 2026.

name: It Is What It Is
description: It Is What It Is is a sports talk show hosted by Harlem rappers Cam'ron and Ma$e — childhood friends and former Children of the Corn groupmates who reunited after a long feud — with co-host Treasure 'Stat Baby' Wilson. Launched in February 2023 on Cam'ron's self-funded Come And Talk 2 Me network, the show mixes sports debate with hip-hop humor and Harlem vernacular. In August 2023 the hosts signed an eighteen-month, eight-figure deal with Underdog Fantasy, reported at twenty million dollars, after Cam'ron said he had invested roughly a quarter of a million dollars of his own money to start the show. Within its first year the network was credited with more than 100 million views and over 600,000 YouTube subscribers. CultureTechLens's Short covers the show; Cam'ron and Ma$e remain further gaps in the graph, named in this packet.

name: IMO with Michelle Obama
description: IMO with Michelle Obama is a weekly advice podcast hosted by former First Lady Michelle Obama and her brother Craig Robinson. Produced by Higher Ground, the media company founded in 2018 by Barack and Michelle Obama, the show was announced in March 2025 around South by Southwest and launched on March 12, 2025, with two episodes — an introductory conversation and an episode featuring actor and writer Issa Rae — with new episodes following weekly. Episodes are built around listener questions about family, relationships, work, and everyday decisions, answered by the sibling hosts with guests drawn from entertainment, sports, and public life. The series was Higher Ground's first video podcast, promoted with a live taping at SXSW in Austin on March 13, 2025. CultureTechLens profiled the show in Short #80, published October 13, 2026; the show had no CultureTechLens entity record before this packet.

name: IShowSpeed
description: IShowSpeed (Darren Jason Watkins Jr., born January 21, 2005, in Cincinnati, Ohio) is an American streamer and recording artist whose chaotic, high-energy broadcasts made him one of the most-watched creators in the world. Watkins created his YouTube channel in 2016 and began streaming in December 2017; his audience exploded in 2021, and he won Breakout Streamer of the Year at the 2022 Streamy Awards. Signed to Warner Records, his 2022 single 'World Cup' became a global streaming hit tied to the tournament. He won Streamer of the Year at both the 2024 and 2025 Streamer Awards, and his in-person world tours have drawn stadium-scale crowds; platform-reported figures put his YouTube channel above 60 million subscribers in October 2026. CultureTechLens profiled IShowSpeed in Short #90, published October 13, 2026.

name: I Never Knew You at All
description: I Never Knew You at All is a novel by Christine Pride and Jo Piazza, published by Atria Books on October 13, 2026 — the third collaboration by the pair, after We Are Not Like Them (2021) and You Were Always Mine (2023). Its protagonist, Simone Hartwell, is a Black former journalist who left her career to raise her son inside her husband Alex's wealthy white family, which is preparing to hand him its grocery business. When her college first love Kwame returns — now the successful journalist she once expected to be — his investigation into the decades-old disappearance of a young Black man from the elite Tate School, the prep school generations of Hartwells attended, forces a reckoning over race, loyalty, forgiveness and the marriage itself. CultureTechLens covered the novel's publication in Short #135, published October 14, 2026.

name: Indianapolis Athletics
description: The Indianapolis Athletics were a Negro leagues baseball club from Indianapolis, Indiana, that played a single season, 1937, as a charter member of the newly founded Negro American League. The club played its home games at Perry Stadium and did not return for 1938, when a new Indianapolis ABCs took the city's place in the league. Two statistical authorities disagree about the club's record, and both figures are carried here rather than blended: Baseball-Reference's register credits the Athletics with a 17–21–1 record and a fourth-place finish in the eight-team league, while the Baseball-Reference Bullpen, drawing on John Holway and James Riley, gives 16–20 and sixth place. The sources also differ on who managed the club: the register and the team's encyclopedia entry name Ted Strong, its leading hitter, as player-manager, while the Bullpen names Sam Crawford. The Athletics are a distinct club from the Indianapolis ABCs, the longer-running Indianapolis team of the earlier Negro National League, and from the ABCs revived in 1938; this record covers only the 1937 Athletics and only what the cited sources support about them.

name: Illinois Institute of Technology
description: The Illinois Institute of Technology (Illinois Tech) is a private research university in Chicago, created in 1940 by the merger of Armour Institute and Lewis Institute. Armour grew from minister Frank Wakeley Gunsaulus's 1890 'Million Dollar Sermon' on the South Side: Philip Danforth Armour Sr. gave $1 million to found it, and when Armour Institute opened in 1893 it offered professional courses in engineering, chemistry, architecture, and library science. Lewis Institute, established in 1895 on Chicago's West Side from the estate of Allen C. Lewis, offered liberal arts as well as science and engineering to men and women. The two boards voted to merge on October 26, 1939, and a Cook County circuit court decision on April 23, 1940, solidified the creation of Illinois Tech. Its main campus stands at 10 West 35th Street in Chicago's Bronzeville neighborhood, where Ludwig Mies van der Rohe directed the architecture program from 1938 to 1958 and designed much of the campus; part of the 120-acre campus entered the National Register of Historic Places in 2005.

name: I Put a Spell on You
description: "I Put a Spell on You" is a 1956 song written by Jalacy "Screamin' Jay" Hawkins, who first recorded it as a ballad for Grand Records in late 1955 in a version not released at the time, then re-recorded it the following year for Columbia's Okeh Records. Hawkins recalled that producer Arnold Maxin brought food and drink into the session and that the band produced the wild, theatrical performance that became his signature: a screamed, menacing delivery far from the straight love ballad originally intended. American Songwriter's history of the song records that the recording caused a stir on release, that Hawkins leaned into the theatrics in live performance, and that the song failed to chart for Hawkins himself. Its afterlife came through covers. Nina Simone made it the title track of her 1965 Philips album I Put a Spell on You, and her version reached No. 23 on the Billboard Hot R&B chart in 1965; Creedence Clearwater Revival, the Alan Price Set, Annie Lennox, and many others have also recorded it. Hawkins's recording was later selected as one of the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame's 500 Songs That Shaped Rock and Roll.

name: Illinois Writers' Project
description: The Illinois Writers' Project was the Illinois unit of the Federal Writers' Project, the Works Progress Administration program that employed out-of-work writers during the Great Depression, operating in Illinois from 1935 to 1943 under director John T. Frederick of Northwestern University. One of the few racially integrated project sites in the country, the Chicago office gathered an extraordinary roster that included Richard Wright, Margaret Walker, Arna Bontemps, Nelson Algren, Willard Motley, Saul Bellow, and Studs Terkel. Its official work produced Illinois guidebooks for the American Guide Series, while the time and wages it provided let Wright develop the ideas behind Native Son and Algren write his breakthrough novel. A special division of the project, headed by Bontemps and Jack Conroy, produced The Negro in Illinois, a sweeping staff-written history of Black life in the state whose chapters covered slavery, the Great Migration, politics, religion, literature, and the performing arts. That manuscript went unpublished when the project was canceled in 1942 and appeared only in 2013, edited from the project's papers.

name: Ilhan Omar
description: Ilhan Omar, born 4 October 1982 in Mogadishu, Somalia, is a Somali-American politician who has represented Minnesota's 5th congressional district — Minneapolis and surrounding suburbs — in the U.S. House of Representatives since 2019. The youngest of seven children, she fled Somalia's civil war with her family at the age of eight, spent four years in a refugee camp in Kenya, and was granted asylum in the United States in 1995; the family settled in Minneapolis in 1997, and she became a U.S. citizen in 2000. She graduated from North Dakota State University in 2011 with degrees in political science and international studies, worked as a nutrition specialist and a Minneapolis City Council policy aide, and in 2016 was elected to the Minnesota House of Representatives, the first Somali American to serve there. Elected to Congress in 2018, she became the first African refugee and one of the first two Muslim women elected to Congress, and the first woman of color to represent Minnesota. Reelected in 2020, 2022 and 2024, she remained in the House in October 2026, seeking another term in the midterm elections.

name: I Am Not Your Negro
description: I Am Not Your Negro is a 2016 documentary film directed by Raoul Peck, based on James Baldwin's unfinished manuscript Remember This House. In 1979 Baldwin wrote to his literary agent describing the book, which would recount the lives and successive assassinations of his friends Medgar Evers, Malcolm X and Martin Luther King Jr. Baldwin died in 1987 without completing it, leaving only thirty pages, and the unfinished manuscript was entrusted to Peck by Baldwin's estate. Peck built the film exclusively around Baldwin's words, matching them with archival footage of the Civil Rights and Black Power movements and connecting those struggles to present-day movements. Samuel L. Jackson narrates Baldwin's text. The film premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival on September 10, 2016, and opened in the United States on February 3, 2017. It was nominated for Best Documentary Feature at the 89th Academy Awards and won the BAFTA Award for Best Documentary. The Museum of Modern Art describes it as a meditation on what it means to be Black in America, framed as a radical narration about race in America.

name: India Love
description: India Love, born India Westbrooks on 3 February 1996 in California, is an American social media influencer, model and recording artist. Raised between Compton and Corona, she first gained attention in 2011 and 2012 by posting photographs on Tumblr alongside her sister Crystal, building an audience before influencer work was an established career path. She moved that following to Instagram and, with her sisters, collectively known as the Westbrooks, starred in the BET reality series The Westbrooks, which premiered in 2015; Ebony reported that she was then the most popular of the sisters on social media, with 1.1 million Instagram followers. She went on to model for brands, appear in will.i.am's 'Boys & Girls' music video in 2016 and release her own singles, including 'Loco' in 2018, under will.i.am's mentorship. In May 2025 she served as an instructor, teaching a Love and Relationships course, at Kai Cenat's Streamer University, and she remains an active streamer and influencer.

name: Ira Aldridge
aliases: Ira Frederick Aldridge; The African Roscius
description: Ira Frederick Aldridge, born July 24, 1807, in New York City to free Black parents, was the first African American actor to achieve success on the international stage. Educated at New York's African Free School, he joined the African Grove Theatre, the all-Black troupe founded in 1821, and apprenticed under James Hewlett, the first African American Shakespearean actor. Facing American hostility to Black performances of white-authored plays, he emigrated to Europe in 1824 and debuted in London in 1825 as Othello, a role he remained associated with for life. Critics' comparison to the Roman actor Roscius gave him the stage name he embraced, the African Roscius. He performed Othello, King Lear, Macbeth, and The Merchant of Venice across Britain, freely adapting classical plays, and from 1852 toured continental Europe — Prussia, Germany, Austria, Switzerland, Hungary, and Poland — receiving honors including the Prussian Gold Medal for Arts and Sciences. He died August 7, 1867, on tour in Łódź, Poland, aged sixty. Memorial plaques honor him at the Royal Shakespeare Theatre in Stratford-upon-Avon and in Łódź.

name: Imani Perry
description: Imani Perry is an American interdisciplinary scholar of race, law, literature, and African American culture. Born September 5, 1972, in Birmingham, Alabama, she moved with her family to Cambridge, Massachusetts, at age five. She earned a B.A. in American studies and literature from Yale College, a Ph.D. in the history of American civilization and a J.D. from Harvard University, and an LL.M. in nineteenth-century property and contract law from Georgetown Law. She taught at Rutgers School of Law for seven years and at Princeton University before joining Harvard's faculty in 2023, where she is the Henry A. Morss Jr. and Elisabeth W. Morss Professor of Studies of Women, Gender and Sexuality and of African and African American Studies and a Carol K. Pforzheimer Professor at the Harvard Radcliffe Institute. Harvard's Radcliffe Institute lists her as the author of nine books, including May We Forever Stand: A History of the Black National Anthem (2018), Looking for Lorraine (2018), Breathe: A Letter to My Sons (2019), South to America (2022), which won the 2022 National Book Award for Nonfiction, and Black in Blues (2025). She received a MacArthur Fellowship in 2023 and also writes for The Atlantic.

name: Iisha Scott
description: Iisha Scott is a meteorologist with NBC Chicago (WMAQ, NBC 5), credited in the station's own coverage as an NBC 5 Storm Team meteorologist. An award-winning Certified Broadcast Meteorologist holding the AMS seal, she earned a BS in Mass Communications from Norfolk State University and a BS in Geosciences/Broadcast Meteorology from Mississippi State University, and joined NBC Chicago in August 2021 from WCNC Charlotte, where she was a weekend meteorologist. She was named to WVON's 40 Under 40 Game Changers Class of 2026.
